chapter.title: The Clinical Room
chapter.sub: Telehealth carts freeze mid-consult — only in three rooms, only on weekday mornings.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the series plan · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 5 · EPISODE 2 · DRAFT · CASE-026  Parallel lenses · Dr. Hale, Maya and Tomas · Level L4 · Intermediate support  Telehealth carts freeze mid-consult in three renovated clinic rooms — only on weekday mornings. The fix is on a network Maya can’t touch, in rooms she can’t enter while a patient is there.  ⚑ RV-125: patient privacy. RV-121: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: The Clinical Room
items.stakes: Patients hang up on their doctors when the picture freezes. The fix lives on a network Maya can't touch, in rooms she can't enter while anyone is being cared for.
items.reward: Carts that work at the busiest hour. Dr. Hale's trust. Tomas's respect. Labels that tell the truth.

objectives.text: Look closer: two things about the rooms

items.rumor: Three rooms. The fourth one, next door, never freezes. What's different about the wall?

items.text: Cold open — “He thought she'd walked out”

items.alt: A clinic consult room seen from the doorway: the telehealth cart's screen shows a frozen doctor with a red FROZEN label. The patient's chair is out of view behind the curtain.
items.caption: 9:38. Somewhere behind that curtain, a patient is waiting for a sentence to finish.

lines.text: I've had an eighty-year-old farmer hang up on a cardiologist because the cardiologist froze mid-sentence. He thought she'd walked out.
Then he didn't hear the rest of what she had to say.

items.alt: Dr. Imogen Hale in the clinic corridor, on the phone to Maya in the AV office.

bubbles.text: C-104 again. Only the three rooms we renovated. Only mornings. Afternoons are perfect.
Is a patient on the call right now?

items.prompt: Can't you just step in and look at the cart? The patient won't mind.

options.label: “Not while she's being seen. Put her on the phone fallback — I'll find it from outside the room.”
options.reply: …Good answer. Our privacy officer would have had us both for breakfast.

options.label: “Just for a second.”
options.reply: Then I'd have to ask her permission, in the middle of a heart consult. No.

options.label: “Is there a room I can test in without a patient?”
options.reply: The sim lab. Meet Mr. Paulsen — our training manikin. He never hangs up.

items.prompt: 9:41. The consult in C-104 is frozen now, the patient still in the room. What do you do first?
known: ◉ A patient is on the call
items.risk: A patient's care — and her privacy.
timeout: The picture stays frozen. The patient hangs up.
Doing nothing is a decision too.

hints.text: Whose room is it while she's being seen?

options.label: Go to C-104 and look at the cart
options.result: Dr. Hale meets you at the door: “Not during a consult.”
options.consequence: The room belongs to the patient while she's being seen.
options.fail: Never enter a room during a patient's consult.

options.label: Ask Dr. Hale to move the patient to the phone fallback; investigate from outside
options.result: The cardiologist finishes on the phone. The patient stays. You open the cart's admin view from the AV office.
options.consequence: Care continues; the evidence comes from outside the room.

options.label: Reboot the cart remotely
options.result: The consult drops completely. The patient hangs up.
options.consequence: The only call you had, gone.
options.fail: Never reboot a live clinical call.

options.label: Ask Tomas to lift the guest cap for everyone
options.result: Tomas: “Every phone in the waiting room would compete with clinical video. No.”
options.consequence: A bigger risk than the one you have.
options.fail: Network policy belongs to its owner.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #43 · AVERY'S LENS  Labels are claims; the system is the evidence  When the label and the system disagree, believe the system — then fix the label.  Three wall ports said CLINICAL. The switch said GUEST. Six weeks of frozen consults followed the label.

items.alt: In the AV office, the cart's own network page: link up, VLAN 300 GUEST, a 4 Mb/s cap, no QoS, a 3.8 Mb/s stream. Maya points at the VLAN line.
items.caption: The cart knows where it is. The wall doesn't.

items.alt: A bitrate graph for the carts over a weekday: steady at the top except between 9 and 11 a.m., where it drops again and again — shaded red.
items.caption: Hardware doesn't keep office hours.

items.title: A different label maker
items.body: C-108 — the room that never freezes — has port labels in the hospital's old typeface. C-104, C-106 and C-110 have new, glossy labels from the renovation contractor. Same words. Different hands.

items.title: Only between nine and eleven.
items.body: The drops line up exactly with the waiting room's guest Wi-Fi peak — patients and families on their phones while they wait. The carts are sharing the guests' uplink and their per-device cap. A failing cart would fail all day.
items.label: Test: what does this point to — and rule out?

items.alt: C-104 at 10:00, empty of patients. On the exam bed sits the simulation lab's training manikin, 'Mr. Paulsen'. Dr. Hale introduces him.

bubbles.text: Meet Mr. Paulsen. Forty years of test calls and he's never once complained about the food.

items.caption: 10:02. The test call freezes — exactly like the consults.

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Tomas and Maya beside a board. Link use: traffic over link speed, times a hundred. On the guest network every device is capped at four megabits. A consult stream at three point eight is ninety-five percent of the cap. Any spike freezes it. And it's my network, so the fix is my change. Bring me the numbers.

bubbles.text: Link use: traffic over link speed, times a hundred. On the guest network every device is capped at four megabits.
A consult stream at three point eight is ninety-five percent of the cap. Any spike freezes it.
And it's my network, so the fix is my change. Bring me the numbers.

items.caption: Intermediate: the formula and what every letter means. The arithmetic is yours.

items.text: 📗 FIELD NOTES · INTERMEDIATE  Terms   QoS   VLAN   Guest network   Formula and variables   ƒ FORMULA · Link utilization  % = traffic ÷ link speed × 100   traffic  Mb/s on the link  link speed  Mb/s the port can carry     ƒ FORMULA · Percentage  % = part ÷ whole × 100   part  the piece you are measuring  whole  everything it is part of

items.prompt: 10:10. You're at Tomas's desk in network engineering. What do you bring him?
timeout: You leave Tomas's desk without asking for anything specific.
An owner can only act on what you bring.

hints.text: What would let Tomas act in two minutes?

options.label: “The carts freeze. Can you look at the network?”
options.result: Tomas: “Everything's up on my side.” He's right — it is up.

options.label: The cart's network page, the morning/afternoon graph, and the manikin test call — ports 4, 6 and 10
options.result: Tomas checks his switch: those ports are GUEST. “And the wall says CLINICAL? Your label's lying.”
options.consequence: Evidence the owner can act on in two minutes.

options.label: “Give me the switch login and I'll fix it.”
options.fail: Never ask for another team's admin keys.

options.label: “Let's replace the carts.”
options.result: Forty thousand dollars for carts that work fine in C-108.

items.title: Medicine over a wire
items.body: In the late 1950s, clinicians at the Nebraska Psychiatric Institute began using two-way closed-circuit television to link a hospital with patients and students elsewhere. The picture was grainy and the link was a dedicated line, but the idea held: care could travel even when people couldn't. Every telehealth cart since depends on the same thing — a path the call can trust.

items.alt: Tomas's switch view: ports 4, 6 and 10 on VLAN 300 (guest); port 8 — C-108, the room that works — on VLAN 210 (clinical).

bubbles.text: Four, six, ten: guest. Eight: clinical. Your working room is the only one patched right.

lines.text: People usually come to me with 'the network's slow'. You came with a VLAN, a port and a graph.
I was raised by a man who labeled his coffee mug.

items.title: The label said CLINICAL.
items.body: The renovation contractor relabeled the ports from the drawing — which showed the intended VLANs, not what was patched. Six weeks of frozen consults followed a label. The switch told the truth the whole time.
items.label: Test: what do you trust — and what must change?

items.alt: System View: cart C-104's port, labeled CLINICAL, is patched to the GUEST VLAN with a 4 Mb/s cap and an uplink shared with the waiting room's Wi-Fi at 94%.
items.caption: Same cart, same wall. Different VLAN, different rules.

items.label: **Fix it:** prepare Tomas's change — put the carts back on the clinical network.

items.alt: 10:30, the busiest hour. Another test call with Mr. Paulsen in C-104 — smooth for the whole ten minutes. Dr. Hale and Maya watch the cart.

bubbles.text: Ten minutes at the worst hour of the day. Not a single freeze.
Now C-106 and C-110. Same test, same hour.

items.prompt: Thursday. How do you stop the next renovation doing this to another wing?
items.happening: All three rooms proven at the peak.
items.risk: The same freeze in the east wing.
timeout: The east wing reopens in May — untested.

hints.text: What should have happened before the rooms reopened?

options.label: No clinical room reopens until every port is checked against Tomas's map and a test call runs at a busy hour
options.result: Facilities adds it to the reopening checklist; Tomas adds a port-map step.
options.consequence: Reopening becomes a proof, not a date.

options.label: Tell the contractor off
options.result: They apologize and do it again in the next wing.

options.label: Label every port yourself
options.result: You relabel 900 ports over a month and get six wrong.
options.consequence: Labels without a check are just newer claims.

options.label: Nothing — the carts work now
options.result: The east wing renovation finishes in May.
options.fail: Fixing the rooms doesn't fix the reopening.

items.label: **Clue Board:** only weekday mornings — which clues separate the explanations?

items.caption: The consult travels in its own lane now.

items.title: Page 14 · 'ports relabeled per drawing'
items.body: The contractor relabeled the ports from the renovation drawing — which showed the intended VLANs, not the ones patched. Nobody tested a call before the rooms reopened. Maya adds a line to the reopening checklist: *a test call, at a busy hour, from every clinical port.*

items.alt: Dr. Hale and Maya in C-104 after clinic hours; the cart is on, showing a green 'call quality: good' banner.

bubbles.text: The farmer's back next week. The cardiologist asked me to tell whoever fixed it that she finished her sentence.
Tell her the label maker's on notice.

items.alt: Hall B, a tiered lecture hall, with the blue hearing-loop sign by the door. Farah, the disability services coordinator, stands at the front.

bubbles.text: A student has sat in row ten of Hall B all semester. Today she told me she's heard maybe half of every lecture. The sign on the door says she should hear everything.

items.caption: Next: *Loop.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  A label is a claim; the device and the switch are evidence. Put the person being cared for first, test with a stand-in instead of a patient, bring the network owner the VLAN, the port and the graph — and prove the fix at the busiest hour.
REFLECTION (optional)  · The contractor relabeled from the drawing, not from the switch. Where in your work does the plan get mistaken for what was built?
